uncited: Hybrid and multi-mode rendering addresses the limitations of pure volume or pure surface rendering by combining them to leverage the strengths of each.

It sets itself apart from pure volume rendering by using surface geometry to clip or guide volume integration, and from pure surface rendering by retaining the ability to render internal volume structures or neural radiance fields behind or within the surface boundary [2165-multi-mode-rendering-with-iso-surfaces-and-meshes, 8367-hybrid-isosurface-dvr-rendering, 11555-mesh-based-neural-rendering].
The core detection logic relies on the isosurface condition.
For a scalar field $f(\mathbf{p})$, the surface is defined by $f(\mathbf{p}) = \tau$.
Upon detection, the intersection position is often refined (e.g., via linear interpolation or binary search) to reduce discretization artifacts [S3, unofficial][S6, unofficial].

The final color is computed using local lighting models (ambient, diffuse, specular) and potentially ambient occlusion or shadows, with no contribution from voxels behind the surface [S3, unofficial][S5, unofficial].
Hybrid and multi-mode rendering techniques have evolved to address the computational complexity of rendering high-fidelity volumetric data alongside explicit geometry.

The integration of surface clipping for volume rendering allows for efficient handling of occlusion, while the combination of isosurface detection with DVR enables realistic visualization of internal structures in medical and scientific imaging.
